blocks.text: [II, 564] There is now no need to say how pleased Noah was to see the dove returning with an olive leaf in its mouth. From this he inferred two things. 1. What the Prophet observes: that the land had been relieved of the waters, that is, not only the highest mountains, whose summits had appeared long before (Gen. VIII, 5.), but also the level places, or at least the hills, in which olives most delight. Columella, book 6, chapter 6: But it (the olive) loves neither low-lying places nor steep ones, but rather moderate slopes, such as we see in Italy among the Sabines, or in the whole province of Baetica. Palladius, book 3, chapter 18: In hot places it delights in a northern hill, in cold places in a southern one. It takes pleasure in middling slopes. It tolerates neither the lowest place nor a steep one, rather moderate slopes, such as the Sabine region or Baetica (read it rather loves moderate slopes). Florentinus, book 9 of the Geoponica, in the chapter Περὶ ἀέρος ἐπιτηδείου ἐλαίας καὶ γῆς σχημάτιον [Peri aeros epitēdeiou elaias kai gēs schēmation], On the air suitable for the olive and on the shapes of the ground: Συναίρεται δὲ τῇ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπιτηδειότητι καὶ τὰ τῆς γῆς σχήματα προσκλινῆ καὶ ὑψηλά. Αἱ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις τόποις, διὰ τὸ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνέμων καταψύχεσθαι· τὸ ὑπερβάλλον τοῦ ἡλίου πυρῶδες, κάλλιστον ἔλαιον ποιοῦσι. [Synairetai de tē tou aeros epitēdeiotēti kai ta tēs gēs schēmata prosklinē kai hypsēla. Hai gar en tois toioutois topois, dia to hypo tōn anemōn katapsychesthai; to hyperballon tou hēliou pyrōdes, kalliston elaion poiousi.] Sloping and elevated shapes of ground also contribute to the suitability of the air. For those that are in such a situation, because the excessive heat of the sun is cooled by the winds, produce the finest oil. Perdicca, in the Themes of Jerusalem, p. 71:
Ὄρος μικρὸν ἀνεστηκώς ἐστι τοῦ Ἐλαιῶνος, [Oros mikron anestēkōs esti tou Elaiōnos,] [col. 31]
The small mount of Olivet rises up. And a little later,
Πρὸς δέ γε τὸ μεσαίτατον μέρος τοῦ ὄρους τούτου Ὁ Ἐλαιῶν κατάκαρπος ὑπὲρ τὴν φύσιν ὄντως. [Pros de ge to mesaitaton meros tou orous toutou Ho Elaiōn katakarpos hyper tēn physin ontōs.]

Toward the middle part of that mount the olive grove is fruitful wholly beyond nature. A small mount, that is, a hill, in the middle of which olives grow. This is just what Palladius had said, that they take pleasure in middling slopes. Second, Noah learned from this that the earth had not been so devastated by the waters of the flood that some fruit-bearing trees did not still survive, on which men and beasts might feed after the flood. For from the olive a judgement could be made about the rest. Indeed, the fact that the dove had returned not at once, as before, but only toward evening, suggested that it had found places where it could rest. For it was not credible that it had flown the whole day. Yet in the evening it flew back to the ark, either because resting on the branches of trees did not seem comfortable enough, or for lack of food, or from longing for its mate and its young, if it had any, or finally because God so provided, that by its return it might refresh Noah's anxious mind and rouse him to hope of an imminent deliverance. But when it was sent out a third time after seven days, it did not return to the ark any more, because then, as the waters receded more and more, it lacked neither food nor a nest in which to hide. From this it was perceived that the waters had ceased.
